summary.title: Effective Spaced Repetition
summary.one_liner: Learn concrete rules for turning facts into atomic, two-way, well-linked flashcards so spaced repetition actually sticks in long-term memory.
keywords: how to write good anki cards
how do i turn notes into flashcards
takeaways: Write short, atomic flashcards: one small piece of information per card, since large cards are hard to recall and hard to grade honestly.
Ask every fact in both directions (term to definition and definition to term) and in multiple ways, including formal and informal forms.
Only memorize what you already understand; write tentative cards in a scratchpad and refine them before committing.
Organize decks by source (book, chapter, lecture notes) rather than trying to build a perfect topic ontology.
Build hierarchies by asking top-down and bottom-up questions, and use list/sequence card templates to learn ordered material.
summary.summary: The author, Fernando Borretti, explains how he uses spaced repetition (mainly with Anki) and why most people struggle to write effective flashcards. The page lists a set of rules: understand first, be honest when grading, keep reviews fun, repeat yourself, organize by source, write atomic and two-way cards, ask questions in multiple ways, and build hierarchies and sequences. Most of the article is worked examples from geology, plate tectonics, neuroscience, vector spaces and group theory, showing how a passage is broken into question/answer cards. The page also covers habit formation and the failure mode of skipped reviews piling up.
